questions.q: A primigravida at 34 weeks presents with BP 168/110 mmHg, proteinuria of 3+, and a severe frontal headache. Which action is the nurse’s priority?
options: Encourage ambulation to reduce oedema
Start continuous fetal monitoring and prepare for possible magnesium sulphate as ordered
Give oral antihypertensives only and discharge home
Restrict all fluids to 500 mL/day
questions.explanation: Severe pre-eclampsia requires stabilisation, seizure prophylaxis (MgSO4), and fetal monitoring. Ambulation and early discharge are unsafe.

questions.q: A woman at 32 weeks reports painless bright-red vaginal bleeding. The nurse’s first action should be to:
options: Perform a digital vaginal examination to assess cervical dilatation
Place the woman in left lateral position, assess maternal vital signs and fetal heart rate, and notify the clinician
Encourage pushing if she feels pressure
Insert a Foley catheter immediately
questions.explanation: Painless bright-red bleeding suggests placenta praevia. Digital VE is contraindicated until placenta location is known. Priorities are maternal/fetal assessment and notification.

questions.q: A client with gestational diabetes is taught to monitor blood glucose. Which statement indicates she understands the teaching?
options: I only need to check my sugar if I feel dizzy
I should check fasting and post-meal levels as advised and report persistent highs
Insulin means I can eat freely without monitoring
Urine testing alone is enough in pregnancy
questions.explanation: GDM management requires structured glucose monitoring and reporting abnormal values; diet and medication adjustments depend on those readings.

questions.q: At 28 weeks a woman reports decreased fetal movements for 24 hours. The most appropriate nursing response is to:
options: Reassure her that movements normally decrease near term
Advise her to come in today for fetal assessment (e.g. kick count review, CTG/ultrasound as ordered)
Tell her to wait another 48 hours
Schedule a routine visit in two weeks
questions.explanation: Reduced fetal movements need prompt evaluation. Reassurance without assessment risks missing fetal compromise.

questions.q: A multipara at 36 weeks has sudden abdominal pain, dark vaginal bleeding, and a tense, tender uterus. The nurse suspects abruption. Which finding would most support this and require urgent action?
options: Soft, non-tender uterus and normal fetal heart rate
Board-like uterus, maternal tachycardia, and non-reassuring fetal heart rate
Painless bleeding with a soft uterus
Only mild irregular contractions
questions.explanation: Abruption often presents with pain, dark blood, hypertonic/tender uterus and fetal distress — emergency management is required.

questions.q: A pregnant woman at 24 weeks has a haemoglobin of 8.5 g/dL. Which instruction is most important?
options: Stop all iron because high doses are toxic in pregnancy
Take iron supplements as prescribed with vitamin C–rich fluids and report constipation or black stools as expected effects
Iron is unnecessary if she eats meat once a week
Only folic acid is needed until the third trimester
questions.explanation: Iron deficiency is common; correct supplementation and adherence teaching matter. Black stools are expected; constipation should be managed, not used as a reason to stop therapy without advice.

questions.q: A woman at 30 weeks has a blood pressure of 142/92 mmHg on two occasions, no proteinuria, and no symptoms. The nurse recognises this as most consistent with:
options: Severe pre-eclampsia
Gestational hypertension (or mild hypertension in pregnancy) needing close follow-up
Normal pregnancy blood pressure
Chronic hypertension only if it started after 36 weeks
questions.explanation: BP ≥140/90 after 20 weeks without proteinuria/severe features suggests gestational hypertension and needs monitoring for progression.

questions.q: Which client should the antenatal nurse prioritise for immediate review?
options: 28 weeks, mild ankle oedema, BP 118/70
34 weeks, epigastric pain, visual spots, BP 160/100
20 weeks, mild nausea, weight gain 0.4 kg/week
36 weeks, irregular Braxton Hicks, fetal movements felt
questions.explanation: Epigastric pain, visual disturbance and high BP suggest severe pre-eclampsia — priority over common, benign findings.

questions.q: A woman is Rhesus negative and her partner is Rhesus positive. At 28 weeks she has had no anti-D. The nurse’s priority teaching is that:
options: Anti-D is never needed if the baby is likely Rh positive
Anti-D immunoglobulin is given as recommended in pregnancy and after potentially sensitising events to prevent antibody formation
She must avoid all hospital contact
Only the newborn needs treatment
questions.explanation: Anti-D prophylaxis prevents maternal sensitisation and haemolytic disease in future pregnancies.

questions.q: A primigravida asks why fundal height is measured each visit. The best explanation is:
options: It only checks for twins
It helps detect abnormal fetal growth or liquor volume that may need further investigation
It replaces the need for ultrasound
It measures maternal weight gain only
questions.explanation: Serial symphysis–fundal height aids screening for growth restriction, macrosomia or liquor abnormalities.

questions.q: A woman at 26 weeks has glycosuria on dipstick. The most appropriate next nursing action is to:
options: Diagnose diabetes immediately and start insulin
Arrange confirmatory blood glucose testing as per protocol (e.g. fasting/OGTT pathway)
Ignore it as normal in pregnancy
Advise complete fasting for a week
questions.explanation: Glycosuria warrants proper blood testing; diagnosis is not based on a single urine result.

questions.q: A client with mild pre-eclampsia is managed as an outpatient. Which instruction must the nurse emphasise?
options: Skip clinic if she feels well
Report headache, visual changes, epigastric pain or reduced fetal movements immediately
Increase salt to raise blood pressure
Take aspirin only when BP is high
questions.explanation: Danger symptoms of progression to severe disease must be reported at once.

questions.q: A woman at 18 weeks has vaginal bleeding and a closed cervix; ultrasound shows a viable fetus. This is best described as:
options: Inevitable abortion
Threatened abortion
Complete abortion
Missed abortion
questions.explanation: Bleeding with a closed cervix and viable pregnancy is threatened miscarriage; inevitable implies open cervix/products progressing.

questions.q: During antenatal teaching, which statement about HIV in pregnancy is most accurate for nursing care?
options: ART should be avoided until after delivery
With testing and treatment as per national guidelines, mother-to-child transmission can be greatly reduced
Breastfeeding is always forbidden regardless of guidelines and viral load
Only the baby needs medication
questions.explanation: Timely ART and guideline-based care significantly reduce vertical transmission.

questions.q: A woman at 37 weeks has itching of palms and soles, dark urine, and raised bile acids. The nurse anticipates that the priority concern is:
options: Normal stretch marks
Intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy with risk to the fetus requiring obstetric review
Simple dry skin
Only maternal discomfort without fetal risk
questions.explanation: ICP is associated with fetal risk (including stillbirth); urgent obstetric assessment is needed.

questions.q: A labouring woman at 6 cm has contractions every 2 minutes lasting 60 seconds. The fetal heart rate drops to 80 bpm during a contraction and recovers slowly to baseline after 40 seconds. The priority nursing action is to:
options: Encourage her to push immediately
Reposition to left lateral, stop oxytocin if running, give oxygen as protocol, and call for help
Ignore the tracing as early decelerations are always benign
Perform fundal pressure
questions.explanation: Late/prolonged decelerations suggest uteroplacental insufficiency — intrauterine resuscitation and urgent review are required.

questions.q: Which finding in the second stage should the nurse report immediately?
options: Fetal heart rate 140 bpm between contractions
Green-stained liquor and fetal heart rate 90 bpm lasting 2 minutes
Mild variable decelerations that recover quickly with position change
Maternal urge to push at full dilatation
questions.explanation: Meconium plus prolonged bradycardia indicates possible fetal compromise needing urgent action.

questions.q: A multipara in active labour requests opioids for pain. Which assessment is most important before administration?
options: Preferred baby names
Cervical dilatation and fetal heart rate pattern, and proximity to birth
Maternal shoe size
Partner’s blood group
questions.explanation: Opioids near birth can depress the neonate; stage of labour and FHR status guide safe use.

questions.q: After artificial rupture of membranes, the nurse notes a loop of cord at the introitus. The priority action is to:
options: Push the cord back into the uterus firmly
Call for help, relieve cord pressure (e.g. elevate presenting part), position knee–chest or exaggerated Sims, and prepare for emergency birth
Start oxytocin to speed delivery
Have the mother stand and walk
questions.explanation: Cord prolapse is an obstetric emergency: relieve pressure, call help, and expedite delivery.

questions.q: A woman has been fully dilated for 2.5 hours with adequate contractions; the head is not descending. The nurse’s best action is to:
options: Reassure that this is always normal in primips
Notify the clinician — prolonged second stage needs assessment for obstruction or assisted birth
Increase intravenous fluids only and wait silently
Apply fundal pressure continuously
questions.explanation: Prolonged second stage requires clinical review for disproportion, malposition or need for assistance.

questions.q: Which maternal behaviour in transition (8–10 cm) is expected and should be supported rather than pathologised?
options: Sudden calmness and sleep between all contractions
Nausea, irritability, shaking, and stating she ‘cannot do this’
Complete refusal to change position for 3 hours without distress
Absence of any show or pressure
questions.explanation: Transition often brings nausea, irritability and self-doubt; supportive care is appropriate if FHR and progress are acceptable.

questions.q: Oxytocin infusion is running. Contractions are lasting 90 seconds with less than 30 seconds resting tone between them. The priority nursing action is to:
options: Increase the infusion rate
Stop or reduce oxytocin per protocol, reposition, notify the clinician, and monitor fetus
Give a fluid bolus only and continue the same rate
Encourage closed-glottis pushing
questions.explanation: Tachysystole reduces placental perfusion; oxytocin must be managed immediately.

questions.q: A labouring woman becomes restless, has sudden sharp abdominal pain, and the fetal presenting part rises. The uterus changes shape. The nurse suspects:
options: Normal transition
Uterine rupture until proven otherwise
False labour
Placenta praevia only
questions.explanation: Sudden pain, loss of station and change in uterine shape raise concern for rupture — emergency response.

questions.q: When is the best time to give intramuscular oxytocin for active management of the third stage (as commonly practised)?
options: After the placenta is delivered and inspected
With delivery of the anterior shoulder (or as per local protocol at birth of the baby)
One hour after birth
Only if bleeding exceeds 1000 mL
questions.explanation: AMTSL timing is typically with delivery of the anterior shoulder or immediately after birth per national protocol.

questions.q: A primip has regular contractions for 3 hours but the cervix remains 3 cm (was 3 cm on admission). Membranes intact, FHR normal. The nurse should:
options: Declare failure to progress and prepare for caesarean immediately
Assess contraction quality, maternal position, hydration/emotion, and continue supportive care with ongoing review
Start pushing teaching
Restrict all oral intake permanently
questions.explanation: Latent/early labour needs support and assessment of contraction effectiveness, not automatic caesarean.

questions.q: Which position is generally preferred for a labouring woman with a non-reassuring fetal heart pattern when not contraindicated?
options: Supine with legs elevated
Left lateral or upright positions that improve uterine perfusion
Lithotomy with prolonged breath-holding
Prone flat
questions.explanation: Left lateral and upright positions often improve uteroplacental blood flow.

questions.q: A woman reports a gush of fluid. Nitrazine/pad testing is positive. Which additional assessment is essential?
options: Maternal blood group only
Fetal heart rate, colour/odour of fluid, and maternal temperature, plus time of rupture
Only the father’s preference for birth place
Immediate episiotomy
questions.explanation: After ROM, assess fetal wellbeing, signs of infection, and meconium.

questions.q: During a vaginal examination the nurse feels a pulsating structure beside the head. The priority is to:
options: Continue routine examination without comment
Stop the exam, avoid further manipulation, call for help, and manage as possible cord presentation/prolapse risk
Push harder to complete dilatation assessment
Rupture membranes deliberately
questions.explanation: Pulsation suggests cord; minimise handling and escalate immediately.

questions.q: A labouring client with a history of previous caesarean is having strong contractions. Which symptom must the nurse treat as a warning of possible scar dehiscence?
options: Mild backache relieved by massage
Sudden cessation of contractions, sharp pain, or maternal haemodynamic change
Desire for analgesia
Clear liquor and reactive CTG
questions.explanation: Scar rupture/dehiscence may present with pain change, loss of contractions, or shock — emergency.

questions.q: The partograph shows the alert line crossed and the action line approaching with inadequate cervical progress despite good contractions. The nurse should:
options: Ignore the partograph if the mother is coping
Escalate to the clinician for decision on augmentation, instrumental delivery or caesarean as appropriate
Send the mother home
Stop all monitoring
questions.explanation: Crossing action thresholds requires skilled obstetric decision-making.

questions.q: One hour after vaginal birth, the fundus is boggy above the umbilicus and lochia is heavy with clots. The first nursing action is to:
options: Document and reassess in 2 hours
Massage the fundus firmly, express clots, and call for help while assessing bleeding and vital signs
Start walking the mother to the bathroom
Give oral fluids only
questions.explanation: Uterine atony is the leading cause of PPH; immediate fundal massage and escalation are first-line nursing actions.

questions.q: A postpartum woman reports sudden chest pain, dyspnoea and anxiety on day 2. The priority action is to:
options: Encourage deep breathing exercises only
Sit her up, give oxygen as protocol, assess vital signs, and call for emergency help — suspect PE until proven otherwise
Apply a warm compress to the chest
Reassure that anxiety is normal and leave her alone
questions.explanation: PP period is high risk for thromboembolism; acute respiratory symptoms need emergency response.

questions.q: On day 3 a mother has fever 38.9°C, uterine tenderness, and foul-smelling lochia. The nurse suspects:
options: Normal involution
Endometritis and should notify the clinician promptly
Only breast engorgement
Milk fever that never needs antibiotics
questions.explanation: Fever, tender uterus and offensive lochia suggest endometritis — needs medical review and treatment.

questions.q: A primipara is tearful on day 4, has trouble sleeping, but cares for the baby and has no thoughts of harm. The nurse’s best response is to:
options: Diagnose major depression and separate her from the baby
Explain baby blues are common, provide support, and teach danger signs of postpartum depression
Tell her to stop breastfeeding
Ignore her feelings
questions.explanation: Baby blues are common and self-limiting; support plus red-flag education for PPD is appropriate.

questions.q: Which finding on the first postpartum day needs urgent reporting?
options: Fundus firm at umbilicus, lochia rubra moderate
Saturated pad in 15 minutes, dizziness, BP 88/50
Mild afterpains with breastfeeding
Temperature 37.4°C
questions.explanation: Heavy bleeding with hypotension indicates PPH/shock — emergency.

questions.q: A breastfeeding mother develops a red, wedge-shaped, painful area on the breast and fever. Priority nursing advice includes:
options: Stop breastfeeding on that side permanently
Continue frequent feeding/expression, gentle support, analgesia as advised, and seek review for possible mastitis/antibiotics
Apply ice only and skip feeds
Wean immediately to formula
questions.explanation: For mastitis, continued milk removal is important alongside medical assessment.

questions.q: After a third-degree tear, which instruction is most important?
options: Avoid all analgesia so she can feel healing
Perineal hygiene, stool softeners as advised, pelvic rest, and report severe pain or bowel control problems
Start vigorous exercise on day 1
Insert tampons within 48 hours
questions.explanation: Perineal trauma needs hygiene, bowel management and follow-up for complications.

questions.q: A mother who had a caesarean 12 hours ago has a respiratory rate of 10, is very drowsy, and has received opioids. The priority is to:
options: Give another dose of opioid for incision pain
Support airway/breathing, stimulate, give oxygen as needed, and notify the clinician — possible opioid depression
Encourage her to sleep deeply undisturbed for 6 hours
Start ambulation immediately without assessment
questions.explanation: Opioid-induced respiratory depression is life-threatening; airway and medical review come first.

questions.q: Which mother needs Rho(D) immunoglobulin after birth?
options: Rh-positive mother, Rh-positive baby
Rh-negative mother, Rh-positive baby, within the recommended timeframe if not already sensitised
Any mother with blood group O
Only if the baby is jaundiced
questions.explanation: Rh-negative mothers with Rh-positive infants receive anti-D as indicated to prevent sensitisation.

questions.q: A postpartum check shows a fundus deviated to the right and above the umbilicus. Lochia is moderate. The first action is to:
options: Massage vigorously without further assessment
Assist her to void, then reassess the fundus
Start oxytocin infusion immediately without assessment
Discharge home
questions.explanation: A full bladder displaces the uterus and impairs contraction; voiding often corrects position.

questions.q: Which statement by a new mother indicates correct understanding of lochia?
options: Bright red heavy bleeding with large clots on day 10 is normal
Lochia should gradually lighten from red to pink/brown to yellow-white; sudden heavy bright bleeding is not normal
No discharge should occur after day 2
Foul smell is expected for 6 weeks
questions.explanation: Pattern and smell help detect secondary PPH or infection.

questions.q: A mother plans to bottle-feed. Which nursing action helps suppress lactation comfort safely?
options: Encourage frequent hot showers directed at the breasts and repeated stimulation
Supportive bra, avoid stimulation, cold packs as needed, and analgesia if engorged — per protocol
Bind breasts extremely tightly for a week
Pump every hour to ‘empty completely’ if not breastfeeding
questions.explanation: Avoid stimulation; comfort measures for engorgement if not lactating.

questions.q: On day 5 a mother reports she cannot stop crying, feels worthless, and has thoughts that the baby might be better without her. The priority is to:
options: Tell her this is normal blues and leave
Stay with her, ensure safety of mother and baby, and arrange urgent mental health/obstetric review
Advise exercise only
Stop all visitors permanently without assessment
questions.explanation: Suicidal or harm ideation indicates possible severe PPD/psychosis risk — safety and urgent referral.

questions.q: Which measure best prevents postpartum thromboembolism in a post-caesarean mother?
options: Strict bed rest for 5 days
Early mobilisation, hydration, and prophylactic measures as prescribed
Crossing legs continuously in bed
Dehydration to reduce urine output
questions.explanation: Early ambulation and VTE prophylaxis are key preventive strategies.

questions.q: A mother asks when sexual activity may resume. The best response is:
options: Always within 3 days of birth
After bleeding has settled, tear/caesarean healing allows, and she feels ready — often after postnatal check, as advised by clinician
Never while breastfeeding
Only after complete weaning
questions.explanation: Timing is individual; healing, lochia and readiness guide advice.

questions.q: A newborn at 1 minute is blue, limp, and not breathing. After drying and stimulating, there is still no breathing. The priority is to:
options: Wait another 2 minutes before acting
Open airway and start positive-pressure ventilation as per neonatal resuscitation guidelines
Give glucose water orally first
Bathe the baby immediately
questions.explanation: Effective ventilation is the key step in neonatal resuscitation when the baby is apnoeic.

questions.q: Which newborn finding needs immediate intervention?
options: Acrocyanosis at 20 minutes of life
Grunting, nasal flaring and chest indrawing at rest
Vernix in skin creases
Heart rate 140 bpm
questions.explanation: Respiratory distress signs require urgent assessment and support.

questions.q: A term baby becomes jittery at 3 hours of age. The mother had poorly controlled diabetes. The nurse’s priority action is to:
options: Ignore jitteriness as normal startle
Check blood glucose and treat hypoglycaemia per protocol while keeping the baby warm and fed
Give insulin to the baby
Delay feeding for 6 hours
questions.explanation: Infants of diabetic mothers are at high risk of hypoglycaemia; test and treat promptly.

questions.q: When is the ideal time to initiate breastfeeding in an uncomplicated term birth?
options: After a 4-hour nursery observation only
Within the first hour, with skin-to-skin as able
On day 2 only
After the first bath
questions.explanation: Early initiation supports bonding, thermoregulation and successful lactation.

questions.q: A newborn has not passed meconium by 36 hours of age. The nurse should:
options: Reassure that delay to day 5 is always normal
Report to the clinician — delayed meconium can signal obstruction or other pathology
Give castor oil
Increase formula forcibly
questions.explanation: Failure to pass meconium within ~24–48 hours needs evaluation.

questions.q: Which action is correct during newborn identification?
options: Apply one band after mother is discharged
Verify identity bands on mother and baby before any separation or procedure
Use only the father’s surname verbally
Skip banding for home births that later attend clinic
questions.explanation: Identification checks prevent mix-ups; bands are verified at each separation/return.

questions.q: A baby of a hepatitis B–positive mother should receive:
options: No special care
Hepatitis B vaccine and HBIG as per national schedule as soon as possible after birth
Antibiotics only
Isolation from the mother for 6 weeks
questions.explanation: HBIG + vaccine promptly after birth reduces transmission risk.

questions.q: Phototherapy is ordered for jaundice. Which nursing care is essential?
options: Cover the eyes, maximise skin exposure, monitor temperature and hydration, and continue feeds
Withhold all feeds during treatment
Place clothing over the whole body under lights
Stop phototherapy if the baby cries
questions.explanation: Eye protection, exposure, thermal care and feeding are standard under phototherapy.

questions.q: Apgar score at 5 minutes is 5. The nurse understands that:
options: No further resuscitation steps are ever needed
Ongoing assessment and support are required; Apgar does not dictate every step but low scores need continued care
The baby is guaranteed normal neurodevelopment
Scoring replaces the need for ventilation if the baby is apnoeic
questions.explanation: Low Apgar indicates need for continued resuscitation/assessment; it is not a standalone prognosis tool.

questions.q: A preterm baby is in kangaroo mother care. Which observation needs intervention?
options: Baby pink, flexed, feeding at the breast
Baby apnoeic, pale, and not responding to gentle stimulation
Mother talking softly to the baby
Stable temperature in range
questions.explanation: Apnoea and pallor require immediate stimulation and escalation.

questions.q: Vitamin K is given to newborns primarily to:
options: Prevent ophthalmia neonatorum
Prevent vitamin K deficiency bleeding
Boost immunity against TB
Replace iron stores
questions.explanation: Newborns have low vitamin K; prophylaxis prevents haemorrhagic disease.

questions.q: A mother is concerned because her 2-day-old has yellowish skin. Bilirubin is below treatment threshold and the baby is feeding well. The best nursing action is to:
options: Tell her all jaundice is dangerous and stop breastfeeding
Explain physiological jaundice, support frequent feeding, and teach danger signs to report
Start phototherapy without orders
Advise sunlight as the only treatment always
questions.explanation: Physiological jaundice is common; feeding support and warning signs education are key.

questions.q: Which newborn is at highest risk for hypothermia?
options: Term baby, skin-to-skin on mother, dry and covered
Preterm baby left uncovered on an open trolley after birth
Term baby under a pre-warmed radiant heater
Baby in kangaroo position with hat on
questions.explanation: Preterm and wet/uncovered infants lose heat rapidly.

questions.q: Eye prophylaxis (e.g. tetracycline ointment) is given to prevent:
options: Neonatal jaundice
Ophthalmia neonatorum (e.g. gonococcal)
Congenital cataract only
Retinopathy of prematurity alone
questions.explanation: Prophylaxis targets preventable infectious conjunctivitis acquired at birth.

questions.q: A baby has a cephalohematoma. The nurse should teach the parents that:
options: It will not cross suture lines and usually resolves over weeks; monitor jaundice risk
It always needs surgical drainage on day 1
It is the same as caput and disappears in hours always
Massage will remove it faster and is required
questions.explanation: Cephalohematoma is limited by sutures, resolves slowly, and may contribute to jaundice.

questions.q: A woman in early labour has a BP of 150/98, proteinuria, and complains of upper abdominal pain. The priority is to:
options: Give oral fluids and reassess tomorrow
Escalate as possible pre-eclampsia with severe features; continuous monitoring and obstetric review
Encourage walking in the corridor unsupervised
Administer ergometrine prophylactically now
questions.explanation: Epigastric pain with hypertension/proteinuria is a severe feature — urgent care.

questions.q: Which admission assessment finding in labour is most urgent to report?
options: Cervix 4 cm, membranes intact, FHR 136
FHR baseline 90 bpm with minimal variability
Maternal pulse 88, temperature 36.8°C
Mild show
questions.explanation: Bradycardia with poor variability suggests fetal compromise.

questions.q: A woman receiving magnesium sulphate for severe pre-eclampsia becomes drowsy, has RR 10, and absent deep tendon reflexes. The priority is to:
options: Increase the magnesium infusion
Stop magnesium, support airway/breathing, give calcium gluconate as ordered, and call for help
Give additional opioids for rest
Sit her in a chair
questions.explanation: These are signs of magnesium toxicity; stop the drug and give antidote per protocol.

questions.q: Active management of the third stage aims primarily to reduce:
options: Maternal bonding time
Postpartum haemorrhage risk
Need for breastfeeding
Duration of pregnancy
questions.explanation: AMTSL reduces PPH, a leading cause of maternal death.

questions.q: A postpartum mother saturates a pad in 20 minutes. Fundus is firm and midline. The nurse should next:
options: Assume atony and only massage
Inspect for genital tract trauma / retained tissue and escalate — firm fundus with heavy bleeding suggests trauma
Ignore if BP is normal once
Give oral iron only
questions.explanation: Firm uterus with heavy bleeding points to lacerations or other non-atonic causes.

questions.q: Which newborn feeding cue should the mother respond to early?
options: Only after prolonged continuous crying
Rooting, hand-to-mouth, and soft sounds before frantic crying
Sleeping through the day without feeds for 8 hours in day 1
Refusal of all contact
questions.explanation: Early cues improve latch success and reduce distress.

questions.q: A woman at 29 weeks has regular painful contractions and cervical change. Priority nursing care includes:
options: Sending her home with no follow-up
Tocolysis/steroids/antibiotics as ordered, fetal monitoring, and preparation for preterm birth care
Encouraging her to push
Immediate ergometrine
questions.explanation: Preterm labour management focuses on steroids for lung maturity and specialised care.

questions.q: During neonatal resuscitation, after 30 seconds of effective PPV the heart rate is 40 bpm. The next step per standard algorithms is generally to:
options: Stop all support
Start chest compressions coordinated with ventilation and consider advanced help/drugs as protocol
Only continue drying
Give oral antibiotics
questions.explanation: HR <60 after effective ventilation → compressions.

questions.q: A mother with HIV asks about feeding. The nurse should:
options: Ignore national guidelines and choose randomly
Counsel according to current national guidelines on ART, viral load and feeding options
State breastfeeding is always impossible
State formula is always unavailable so guidelines do not matter
questions.explanation: Feeding counselling must follow current national PMTCT guidance.

questions.q: Which sign indicates true labour rather than false labour?
options: Contractions stop with walking and hydration
Progressive cervical dilatation and contractions that intensify and continue despite rest
Only fetal movements increase
Irregular tightenings without cervical change for days
questions.explanation: Cervical change with progressive contractions defines true labour.

questions.q: A primigravida at term has a blood pressure of 120/80, mild oedema of feet, and physiologic anaemia. The nurse interprets this as:
options: Severe disease needing ICU
Common pregnancy findings needing routine surveillance, not emergency treatment
Indication for immediate induction
Proof of renal failure
questions.explanation: Mild dependent oedema and dilutional anaemia can be physiologic; severe features need action.

questions.q: After birth the nurse dries the baby and places skin-to-skin. This primarily helps to:
options: Delay bonding
Support thermoregulation, bonding and early breastfeeding
Increase infection risk always
Replace the need for any resuscitation assessment
questions.explanation: Skin-to-skin supports temperature, bonding and feeding initiation.

questions.q: A labouring woman has a temperature of 38.5°C, foul liquor, and fetal tachycardia. The priority is to:
options: Continue without informing anyone
Notify the clinician, increase monitoring, and prepare for possible septic work-up and expedited care
Give cold drinks only
Stop all IV access
questions.explanation: Chorioamnionitis features need prompt obstetric management.

questions.q: Which postpartum warning sign should be taught before discharge?
options: Mild sweating at night once
Heavy bleeding soaking a pad in under an hour, severe headache, fever, or calf pain
Baby feeding 8–12 times/day
Mild afterpains
questions.explanation: Danger signs education prevents delayed care for PPH, pre-eclampsia, infection and VTE.

questions.q: A newborn’s heart rate is 70 bpm after drying and stimulation; breathing is absent. The nurse should:
options: Only wrap and wait
Begin PPV immediately
Check blood sugar before any respiratory support
Bathe before resuscitation
questions.explanation: Apnoea with low HR → open airway and ventilate without delay.

questions.q: A woman with PROM at 34 weeks is not in labour. Priority nursing surveillance includes:
options: Ignoring temperature
Monitoring for infection (temperature, pulse, liquor, FHR) and fetal wellbeing
Daily digital exams to check cervix
Mandatory immediate caesarean without steroids consideration
questions.explanation: Expectant management requires infection and fetal surveillance; minimise unnecessary VE.

questions.q: Which action is inappropriate when shoulder dystocia is called?
options: McRoberts position and suprapubic pressure as directed
Applying strong fundal pressure as the first and only manoeuvre
Calling for extra help
Noting time of dystocia
questions.explanation: Fundal pressure is not the first-line manoeuvre and can worsen outcomes.

questions.q: A mother reports her baby sleeps 5 hours between feeds on day 1 and is hard to rouse. Bilirubin risk is moderate. The nurse should:
options: Praise long sleep as always ideal
Wake for feeds, assess hydration/jaundice, and review with the clinician as needed
Start water feeds only
Discharge without feeding review
questions.explanation: Excessive sleepiness can signal inadequate intake or illness.

questions.q: Inverted uterus is suspected after traction on the cord. The priority is to:
options: Continue aggressive traction
Call for help, stop traction, resuscitate mother, and prepare for manual replacement by skilled clinician
Give oral fluids only
Send the mother to the toilet
questions.explanation: Uterine inversion is a haemorrhagic emergency — stop traction and get skilled help.

questions.q: A woman in labour has received epidural analgesia. Which assessment is especially important?
options: Ability to run a marathon mid-labour
Bladder status, BP, sensory level, and fetal heart rate
Only her favourite music
Partner’s temperature
questions.explanation: Epidurals can cause hypotension, urinary retention and alter sensation — structured monitoring is required.

questions.q: Which client is the best candidate for trial of labour after caesarean if other factors are favourable?
options: Prior classical (vertical) uterine incision
One previous low transverse caesarean and adequate pelvis/facility for emergency CS
Prior uterine rupture
Three classical scars
questions.explanation: Low transverse scar and readiness for emergency CS are typical prerequisites; classical scar is a contraindication.

questions.q: A newborn has asymmetric Moro reflex and limited movement of one arm after shoulder dystocia. The nurse should:
options: Force the arm through full range immediately
Support the limb, avoid pulling, and report suspected brachial plexus injury
Ignore until the 6-week visit only
Apply heavy weights to the arm
questions.explanation: Suspected Erb’s palsy needs gentle handling and prompt clinical review.

questions.q: Postpartum haemoglobin is 7.0 g/dL after significant PPH. The mother is dizzy when sitting. Priority care includes:
options: Unsupervised ambulation to the shop
Assisted mobilisation, iron/transfusion as ordered, and monitoring for ongoing bleeding
Restricting all visitors for a month
Stopping breastfeeding permanently
questions.explanation: Symptomatic anaemia after PPH needs safety, replacement therapy and bleeding surveillance.

questions.q: A woman at 8 weeks has unilateral pelvic pain, spotting, and shoulder tip pain. BP 90/60. The priority is to:
options: Diagnose gastroenteritis and send home
Suspect ectopic pregnancy with possible rupture — urgent stabilisation and surgical review
Perform vigorous pelvic exam only
Give high-dose ergometrine
questions.explanation: Shoulder tip pain and shock with early pregnancy symptoms suggest ruptured ectopic.

questions.q: Which practice supports evidence-based care in normal labour?
options: Routine continuous lithotomy from 3 cm for all women
Freedom of movement, continuous support, and monitoring appropriate to risk
Withholding all information about progress
Mandatory enema and shaving for every woman
questions.explanation: Supportive, respectful, mobility-friendly care improves outcomes in uncomplicated labour.

questions.q: A baby is born through thick meconium, is floppy and not breathing. After the initial steps, the priority is:
options: Stimulation only without airway support
Clear airway as indicated and provide PPV if still not breathing — follow current NRP guidance
Routine vigorous suction of a vigorous crying baby only
Delay drying
questions.explanation: Non-vigorous infants need airway support/ventilation per current resuscitation algorithms.

questions.q: Lochia has been pale; on day 12 it becomes heavy and bright red with clots. The nurse should advise:
options: This is always normal menstrual return
Seek care promptly — possible secondary PPH
Double activity level
Ignore unless fever is 40°C
questions.explanation: Sudden heavy bright bleeding after lochia has lightened needs urgent assessment.

questions.q: A pregnant woman with cardiac disease is in labour. Which nursing action is most appropriate?
options: Encourage prolonged closed-glottis pushing in supine position
Position for comfort/cardiac load reduction, monitor closely, and shorten second stage as directed by the team
Withhold all pain relief always
Give unrestricted IV fluid boluses without orders
questions.explanation: Cardiac disease needs careful positioning, monitoring and controlled second stage.

questions.q: Teaching about exclusive breastfeeding for 6 months is based on the understanding that it:
options: Prevents all illness forever
Provides optimal nutrition and protection when practised with appropriate complementary feeding later
Means water must be given daily from birth in all climates
Requires scheduled 6-hour intervals only
questions.explanation: Exclusive breastfeeding for ~6 months is recommended for optimal nutrition and immunity support.

questions.q: A woman with pre-eclampsia on MgSO4 has urine output of 15 mL/hour for 3 hours. The nurse should:
options: Increase magnesium rate
Report oliguria — risk of magnesium toxicity and renal concern; review orders
Give potassium without assessment
Stop monitoring reflexes
questions.explanation: Oliguria with MgSO4 increases toxicity risk; report and review.

questions.q: Which is the correct immediate care after birth of the baby before cord clamping when the baby is vigorous?
options: Immediate routine suction of all vigorous babies’ throats deeply
Dry, keep warm, skin-to-skin if appropriate, assess breathing/tone/HR
Separate from mother for 1 hour always
Delay drying until after weighing
questions.explanation: Warmth, drying and assessment are foundational; vigorous babies do not need deep suction.

questions.q: A postpartum woman has a painful, swollen, red calf and a positive Homans’ sign is mentioned. The safest nursing action is to:
options: Massage the calf firmly
Advise rest of the limb, avoid massage, and notify the clinician to evaluate for DVT
Encourage long walks immediately without review
Apply sequential compression without assessment orders only
questions.explanation: Suspected DVT: do not massage; escalate for diagnosis and treatment.

questions.q: In focussed antenatal care, the nurse prioritises:
options: Only weighing at each visit without history
Risk identification, education, preventive therapies (e.g. TT, iron), and birth preparedness
Avoiding discussion of danger signs
One visit only in the whole pregnancy
questions.explanation: Quality ANC detects risk, prevents disease and prepares for birth/emergency.

questions.q: A woman is pushing; the head delivers but the shoulders do not follow with gentle traction. The nurse should:
options: Pull harder on the head
Call out ‘shoulder dystocia’, note the time, and assist with McRoberts and suprapubic pressure as directed
Apply fundal pressure only
Leave the room to find a form
questions.explanation: Shoulder dystocia needs organised emergency manoeuvres — not stronger axial traction or fundal pressure first.

questions.q: Which newborn temperature is concerning and needs intervention?
options: 36.7°C axillary after skin-to-skin
35.2°C axillary despite warming measures started
questions.explanation: Hypothermia <36.5°C (and especially lower) needs active rewarming and assessment.

questions.q: A mother refuses vitamin K for her newborn. The nurse’s best response is to:
options: Inject without consent
Explain risks of vitamin K deficiency bleeding, document, and involve the clinician while respecting legal/ethical process
Agree that vitamin K is unnecessary worldwide
Discharge without any discussion
questions.explanation: Informed refusal requires clear risk explanation, documentation and appropriate escalation.

questions.q: Which finding after epidural may indicate a serious complication needing urgent review?
options: Mild itching
Sudden severe headache worse when upright after dural puncture risk, or new marked motor block with respiratory difficulty
Wanting a position change
Request for information
questions.explanation: Post-dural puncture headache pattern or high block/respiratory compromise need urgent anaesthetic review.

questions.q: A twin pregnancy at 30 weeks has contractions. Priority teaching/care includes:
options: Assuming preterm birth cannot be delayed or prepared for
Seeking care early, steroids if indicated, and monitoring for preterm labour complications
Heavy lifting to ‘speed engagement’
Avoiding hospital contact
questions.explanation: Multiple pregnancy has higher preterm risk; early care and steroids matter.

questions.q: The nurse notes a postpartum fundus firm but lochia has a foul odour on day 6 with low-grade fever. Priority is to:
options: Document as normal and discharge without review
Report possible infection for assessment and treatment
Start the mother on unsupervised herbal douches only
Stop hygiene measures
questions.explanation: Offensive lochia with fever suggests infection.

questions.q: Which action promotes parent–infant attachment in the first hour?
options: Prolonged separation for routine tasks when the baby is stable
Uninterrupted skin-to-skin and support for the first breastfeed when mother and baby are well
Keeping the baby under lights away from parents for 3 hours routinely
Limiting parental touch
questions.explanation: Early contact supports bonding and breastfeeding success.

questions.q: A woman with severe pre-eclampsia is receiving MgSO4. Which parameter is most important to monitor for toxicity?
options: Hair growth
Respiratory rate, urine output and deep tendon reflexes
Shoe size
Preferred baby name
questions.explanation: RR, reflexes and urine output are classic magnesium toxicity monitors.

questions.q: When counting fetal movements, the nurse should advise the woman to seek care if:
options: She feels 10 movements in 2 hours while resting and focusing, as taught
Movements are clearly reduced from her normal pattern or she cannot achieve the taught count threshold
Movements are stronger in the evening
She feels hiccups
questions.explanation: A sustained reduction from the normal pattern needs same-day assessment.

questions.q: A labouring woman’s membranes rupture and the fluid is green. FHR is 110 with late decelerations. The priority is to:
options: Continue without change
Intrauterine resuscitation measures and urgent clinical review for possible fetal distress
Discharge for home birth
Give a large meal
questions.explanation: Meconium plus non-reassuring FHR requires action.

questions.q: Which mother needs the most urgent mental health referral?
options: Day 3 tearfulness with good infant care
Day 10 inability to sleep, believing the baby is possessed, and refusing to eat
Mild worry about bathing technique
Asking many questions about feeding
questions.explanation: Psychotic features or severe functional change need urgent specialist care.

questions.q: A preterm newborn under a warmer has a temperature of 36.0°C. The nurse should:
options: Undress further for examination only
Increase thermal support, check for infection/hypoglycaemia as indicated, and reassess
Bathe in cool water
Turn the warmer off
questions.explanation: Hypothermia in preterms needs active thermal care and evaluation of causes.

questions.q: During antenatal care, a BP of 150/100 at 22 weeks in a woman whose BP was normal before pregnancy most likely indicates:
options: Normal finding
Gestational hypertension or evolving pre-eclampsia pathway — needs follow-up and investigation
Only white-coat hypertension that is never significant
Hypotension
questions.explanation: New hypertension after 20 weeks requires structured follow-up.

questions.q: A woman is fully dilated and has been pushing for 45 minutes; FHR remains reassuring. The nurse should:
options: Shout continuously at her
Support effective pushing, position changes, and ongoing fetal/maternal monitoring
Start fundal pressure routinely
Stop all encouragement
questions.explanation: Supportive second-stage care with monitoring is appropriate while progress and FHR allow.

questions.q: Which practice reduces neonatal tetanus risk?
options: Unclean cord cutting with household blades
Clean delivery, hygienic cord care, and maternal tetanus toxoid as scheduled
Applying cow dung to the cord
Avoiding all antenatal contact
questions.explanation: Clean birth practices and maternal TT prevent neonatal tetanus.

questions.q: A postpartum mother has BP 170/110, headache, and epigastric pain on day 1. The nurse should:
options: Discharge home with paracetamol only
Treat as possible postpartum pre-eclampsia/eclampsia risk — urgent review and monitoring
Encourage heavy exercise
Stop all antihypertensives if previously prescribed without advice
questions.explanation: Pre-eclampsia can present or worsen postpartum.

questions.q: The nurse explains that the purpose of antenatal iron and folate is mainly to:
options: Induce labour
Prevent and treat anaemia and reduce related risks
Replace the need for malaria prevention
Guarantee a small baby
questions.explanation: Iron/folate reduce anaemia and associated maternal–fetal risks.

questions.q: A newborn has not voided by 30 hours of age. The nurse should:
options: Ignore until day 5
Assess hydration, feeding, and report delayed voiding for evaluation
Give frusemide without orders
Stop all feeds
questions.explanation: Delayed first void needs assessment for adequacy of intake or urinary issues.

questions.q: Which is a danger sign in pregnancy that the woman should report immediately?
options: Mild tiredness after a long day
Vaginal bleeding, severe headache, visual change, or severe abdominal pain
Occasional Braxton Hicks at 36 weeks
Increased vaginal discharge that is clear and non-itchy near term
questions.explanation: Bleeding, severe headache/visual symptoms and severe pain are classic danger signs.

questions.q: A woman in labour is HIV positive on ART. Which care principle is correct?
options: Avoid all standard precautions
Maintain confidentiality, continue ART, and follow national protocols for labour and newborn care
Announce her status to the whole ward
Stop ART during labour always
questions.explanation: Confidential, guideline-based PMTCT care continues through labour and the newborn period.

questions.q: After placental delivery, the nurse inspects the placenta and notes a missing cotyledon. The priority is to:
options: Dispose of the placenta without reporting
Report possible retained products — risk of PPH and infection
Tell the mother to push again for 2 hours
Ignore if bleeding is currently mild
questions.explanation: Incomplete placenta raises risk of retained tissue complications.

questions.q: A mother with sore nipples from poor latch should be advised to:
options: Stop breastfeeding permanently at the first crack
Improve positioning and latch, feed frequently, and seek lactation support; assess for infection if severe
Use only the tip of the nipple in the baby’s mouth
Space feeds to 8 hours to rest
questions.explanation: Most nipple trauma improves with better latch and support.

questions.q: Which Apgar component reflects respiratory effort?
options: Grimace
Heart rate
Respiration
Colour only
questions.explanation: The ‘R’ in Apgar is respiration/respiratory effort.

questions.q: A woman at 39 weeks has a BP of 160/110, proteinuria, and clonus. The priority medication anticipated is:
options: Oral iron only
Magnesium sulphate for seizure prophylaxis as ordered, plus BP management and birth planning
High-dose vitamin C alone
Immediate ergometrine before stabilisation
questions.explanation: Severe pre-eclampsia management centres on MgSO4, BP control and timely birth.

questions.q: During PPH management, after calling for help and fundal massage, the nurse should also:
options: Leave the mother to fetch paperwork first
Ensure IV access, monitor vital signs, give uterotonics as ordered, and keep accurate blood loss assessment
Give only oral fluids
Stop oxygen if used
questions.explanation: Systematic PPH care: help, massage, oxytocics, access, monitoring, quantifiy loss.

questions.q: A newborn of a mother with active TB (not on appropriate treatment) may need:
options: No special consideration
Evaluation per guidelines for infection risk and feeding/separation decisions
Routine discharge without history review
Immediate BCG only with no other assessment ever
questions.explanation: Maternal TB affects newborn infection risk and management planning.

questions.q: Which statement about the latent phase of labour is appropriate?
options: It always requires immediate oxytocin in every woman
It can be longer; support, rest, hydration and monitoring are often appropriate if mother and fetus are well
Cervical checks every 15 minutes are mandatory
Women must lie supine throughout
questions.explanation: Latent labour often needs supportive care rather than aggressive intervention.

questions.q: A post-term woman at 41+ weeks reports reduced movements. CTG is non-reactive. The nurse anticipates:
options: Sending home without review
Further fetal assessment and likely obstetric plan for delivery
Waiting 1 week silently
Only dietary advice
questions.explanation: Post-term pregnancy with reduced movements and non-reactive CTG needs prompt obstetric action.

questions.q: Which newborn is most likely to need glucose monitoring?
options: Term AGA baby, mother without diabetes, feeding well
Infant of diabetic mother, or preterm/SGA baby
Baby with strong cry and pink colour only as risk factors
Baby already 10 days old with good weight gain only
questions.explanation: IDM, preterm and growth-restricted infants are priority groups for glucose checks.

questions.q: A woman develops a seizure in the antenatal ward with BP 180/120. After protecting the airway, the nurse prepares for:
options: Immediate discharge
Magnesium sulphate and emergency obstetric management for eclampsia
Only oral diazepam at home
Ergometrine as first drug
questions.explanation: Eclampsia management prioritises airway, MgSO4 and stabilisation toward birth.

questions.q: The best nursing measure to support a woman with fear of labour is to:
options: Dismiss her fears
Provide clear information, continuous support, and involvement in decisions
Leave her alone for long periods
Promise zero pain without explanation
questions.explanation: Support and information reduce fear and improve labour experience.

questions.q: A mother is hepatitis B positive. Before discharge the nurse verifies that the newborn has received:
options: Only vitamin A
Hepatitis B vaccine and HBIG as indicated, with documentation
No injections of any kind
Only BCG
questions.explanation: Birth-dose vaccine ± HBIG is critical for exposed newborns.

questions.q: Which lochia pattern is abnormal on day 4?
options: Pinkish-brown moderate flow
Sudden return of heavy bright-red bleeding with clots and dizziness
Scant dark discharge
Mild afterpains during feeds
questions.explanation: Recurrent heavy bright bleeding can signal secondary PPH.

questions.q: A labouring woman has a known placenta praevia. Which nursing action is contraindicated?
options: Monitoring maternal vital signs
Digital vaginal examination to ‘check dilatation’
Preparing blood products as ordered
Continuous fetal monitoring as indicated
questions.explanation: Digital VE is contraindicated in known placenta praevia.

questions.q: Kangaroo mother care is especially important because it:
options: Replaces all medical care for extreme preterms always
Supports warmth, breastfeeding, and stability for eligible low-birth-weight babies
Is only for term babies
Requires expensive equipment only
questions.explanation: KMC improves thermal control and feeding for stable LBW infants.

questions.q: A woman reports watery discharge at 30 weeks without contractions. The nurse’s priority assessments include:
options: Only maternal weight
Confirming PROM vs urine/liquor, fetal heart, infection signs, and gestational age–based plan
Immediate pushing teaching
Discharge without review
questions.explanation: Possible preterm PROM needs careful assessment and specialist plan.

questions.q: Which action is appropriate when a newborn is vigorous and crying at birth with clear liquor?
options: Deep pharyngeal suction before drying
Dry and stimulate as needed; no routine deep suction
Separate from mother for 30 minutes routinely
Delay clamping discussion forever
questions.explanation: Vigorous newborns do not need routine deep suction.

questions.q: A postpartum patient has a temperature of 38.2°C on day 1, breast engorgement starting, and a non-tender uterus. The nurse should:
options: Start IV antibiotics without assessment
Assess for other infection sources, support engorgement care, and review if fever persists — early fever needs evaluation
Ignore all fevers in the first week
Stop breastfeeding
questions.explanation: Early fever needs assessment; engorgement alone may contribute but infection must be considered.

questions.q: The partograph is used primarily to:
options: Replace clinical judgement entirely
Graphically monitor labour progress and trigger timely action
Measure only maternal height
Document newborn weight only
questions.explanation: Partograph helps detect prolonged labour and guide intervention timing.

questions.q: A woman with cardiac disease is postpartum. Priority nursing care includes:
options: Encouraging sudden heavy exertion on day 1
Monitoring for fluid overload and cardiac symptoms, graded activity, and medication adherence
Stopping all cardiac drugs without advice
Restricting breastfeeding always
questions.explanation: The postpartum period stresses the cardiovascular system; careful monitoring is required.

questions.q: Which teaching is correct about exclusive breastfeeding and infant stools in the first weeks?
options: No stools for 7 days is always normal
Frequent soft yellow stools are common in exclusively breastfed infants; dry hard stools with poor feeding need review
Stools should always be black after day 5
Water must be added if stools are soft
questions.explanation: Breastfed stool patterns differ from formula; poor output with feeding issues needs review.

questions.q: A woman is receiving oxytocin. Contractions are every 1 minute lasting 80 seconds. Fetal scalp electrode shows prolonged decelerations. The nurse’s first actions include:
options: Increase oxytocin
Stop oxytocin, left lateral position, oxygen per protocol, notify clinician
Start pushing
Give a sedative only
questions.explanation: Tachysystole with fetal compromise → stop oxytocin and resuscitate in utero.

questions.q: Antenatal education on birth preparedness should include:
options: Only buying baby clothes
Recognising danger signs, transport plan, skilled birth attendant, and needed supplies/funds
Avoiding any discussion of emergencies
Planning to birth alone without telling anyone
questions.explanation: Birth preparedness and complication readiness reduce delays in seeking care.

questions.q: A newborn has central cyanosis and respiratory rate of 80. The nurse should:
options: Feed immediately before any assessment
Support airway/oxygen as protocol and call for urgent help
Wrap tightly and ignore colour
Discharge for home monitoring only
questions.explanation: Central cyanosis and tachypnoea are emergencies.

questions.q: Which mother is at highest risk for postpartum haemorrhage?
options: Uncomplicated spontaneous birth, firm uterus, no tears
Prolonged labour, multiple pregnancy, or previous PPH
Primip with short second stage only
Exclusive breastfeeding intent only
questions.explanation: Overdistension, prolonged labour and prior PPH raise PPH risk.

questions.q: A woman in the latent phase asks for caesarean because of fear. The nurse should:
options: Schedule surgery without counselling
Explore fears, provide information and support, and involve the obstetric team in shared decisions
Refuse all conversation
Guarantee labour will be painless
questions.explanation: Fear needs support and informed choice, not automatic surgery or dismissal.

questions.q: Hand hygiene before newborn care is essential mainly to:
options: Satisfy paperwork only
Reduce healthcare-associated infection risk to the neonate
Warm the nurse’s hands only
Replace skin-to-skin
questions.explanation: Newborns are vulnerable to infection transmitted on hands.

questions.q: A woman at 33 weeks has BP 140/90, proteinuria 1+, and no severe symptoms. The nurse anticipates:
options: Immediate home discharge with no follow-up
Close surveillance for progression, fetal assessment, and possible admission depending on protocol
Ergometrine therapy
Unsupervised heavy exercise programme
questions.explanation: Even ‘mild’ pre-eclampsia needs structured surveillance.

questions.q: When assisting with controlled cord traction, the nurse must ensure:
options: Continuous traction without counter-support on the uterus
Counter-traction on the uterus above the pubis and traction only with a contraction when the placenta is separated
Pulling as hard as possible continuously
No observation of blood loss
questions.explanation: Incorrect traction technique risks inversion and trauma.

questions.q: A mother reports her 5-day-old has fewer wet nappies and is lethargic. The nurse should:
options: Reassure without assessment
Assess feeding, weight, jaundice and hydration and refer urgently if dehydration or illness is present
Advise stopping all feeds
Suggest honey water
questions.explanation: Fewer wet nappies and lethargy are danger signs in the neonate.

questions.q: Which postpartum contraceptive teaching is accurate for a fully breastfeeding mother (LAM criteria applying)?
options: LAM is 100% permanent sterilisation
Lactational amenorrhoea can be effective under strict criteria; other methods may be needed as eligibility changes
No method is ever needed while breastfeeding
Combined oral contraceptives are always first choice at 48 hours for everyone
questions.explanation: LAM works only with correct criteria; counselling should cover transition to other methods.

questions.q: A woman with GDM in labour needs:
options: No glucose monitoring because labour cures diabetes
Blood glucose monitoring and insulin/glucose management per protocol to avoid maternal–fetal hypo/hyperglycaemia
High-dose oral sugar continuous infusion without orders
Stopping all diabetes care
questions.explanation: Intrapartum glucose control protects mother and fetus.

questions.q: The nurse suspects postpartum urinary retention when:
options: The mother voids 400 mL freely and fundus is firm midline
Fundus is high and displaced, with small frequent voids or inability to void after birth
Lochia is scant
She requests analgesia for afterpains only
questions.explanation: Displacement and voiding difficulty suggest retention — bladder emptying aids uterine tone.

questions.q: A newborn screening blood spot is best collected:
options: Before any feed ever
As per national timing guidelines (often after 24 hours of age) with correct technique
Only if the parents request research participation
From the mother’s finger only
questions.explanation: Timing and technique affect screening accuracy.

questions.q: Which sign suggests impending eclampsia in a pre-eclamptic woman?
options: Mild ankle swelling alone
Severe headache, visual disturbances, epigastric pain, or hyperreflexia/clonus
Desire to sleep after a long clinic visit
Normal fetal movements
questions.explanation: Neurological and epigastric symptoms warn of progression toward eclampsia.

questions.q: During neonatal resuscitation, room air vs oxygen use should follow:
options: Personal preference only
Current resuscitation guidelines (starting with air for term babies and titrating based on response/targets)
100% oxygen for every term baby for 20 minutes routinely
No oxygen ever for any baby
questions.explanation: Modern NRP guidance uses air initially for term infants with targeted saturation.

questions.q: A multipara delivers a live baby; within minutes she becomes pale, hypotensive, and the uterus is poorly contracted with heavy bleeding. The nurse’s simultaneous priorities are:
options: Documentation only for 10 minutes
Call for help, continuous fundal massage, uterotonics as ordered, IV access/fluids, oxygen, and ongoing vital signs
Walk her to the shower
Delay oxytocin until the placenta is histologically reported
questions.explanation: PPH requires parallel actions: help, mechanical and pharmacological uterine control, and resuscitation.

questions.q: A woman at 25 weeks has a cervical length of 20 mm on ultrasound and a history of previous mid-trimester loss. The nurse anticipates possible:
options: Discharge without follow-up
Closer surveillance and interventions such as progesterone/cerclage as the obstetric team decides
Immediate induction of labour
Advice to run daily marathons
questions.explanation: Short cervix with poor history needs specialist prevention strategies.

questions.q: Which behaviour by staff best supports respectful maternity care?
options: Performing procedures without explanation
Seeking consent, maintaining privacy, and communicating plans in a language the woman understands
Scolding women for expressing pain
Restricting all companions even when policy allows
questions.explanation: Consent, privacy and communication are core to respectful care.

questions.q: A newborn has ambiguous genitalia. The priority nursing approach is to:
options: Assign a gender immediately in front of relatives without senior review
Avoid hasty gender assignment, support parents, and ensure urgent specialist evaluation
Post photos publicly
Discharge without investigation
questions.explanation: Disorder of sex development needs sensitive, specialist-led management.

questions.q: After a forceps birth, the nurse should prioritise assessment for:
options: Only maternal happiness
Maternal genital tract trauma and neonatal marks/neurological behaviour
Skipping the fundus check
Immediate unsupervised bath of mother
questions.explanation: Instrumental birth increases risk of maternal trauma and neonatal injury signs.

questions.q: A mother who is not breastfeeding asks how to manage engorgement. The best advice is:
options: Pump every hour to keep producing milk
Supportive bra, cold packs, minimal stimulation, analgesia if needed
Hot compresses before every pump session to increase supply
Antibiotics routinely without infection signs
questions.explanation: If not lactating, avoid stimulation; comfort measures reduce engorgement pain.
